{{smaller block|Our passions and our interests flov ''philosophize'' us into mere mortals.}} + ''pick''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To pick, open with a pick or other instrument.
{{smaller block|With his craft the dore ''unpicketh.''
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., v.}}}}
'''2.''' To pick out; undo by picking: as, to ''unpick'' stitches.
{{smaller block|It was she herself who, with very great care, and after a long examination of the silk threads, ''unpicked'' the stitches on one side of the letter and sewed them back by means of a hair.
{{right|''R. Hodgson'', Proc. Soc. Psychical Research, III. 377.}}}}
'''3.''' To pick out the stitches of; rip.
{{smaller block|A robe, half-made, and half ''unpicked'' again.
{{right|''W. Collins.''}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To pick out stitches.
{{smaller block|While we boys ''unpicked'', the bigger girls would sew the patchwork covers.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., X. 12.}}}}

'''unpickable''' (un-pik′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''pickable.''] Incapable of being picked, in any sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>How wary they are grown! not a door open now,
But double-barred; not a window,
But up with a case of wood, like a spice-box;
And their locks ''unpickable.''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unpicked''' (un-pikt′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''picked.''] '''1.''' Not picked; not chosen or selected.
{{smaller block|Whatsoever time, or the heedlesse hand of blind chance, hath drawne down from of old to this present, in her huge dragnet, whether Fish, or Sea-weed, Shells, or Shrubbs, ''unpickt'', unchosen, those are the Fathers.
{{right|''Milton'', Prelatical Episcopacy.}}}}
'''2.''' Unplucked; ungathered, as fruit.
{{smaller block|Now comes in the sweetest morsel of the night, and we must hence and leave it ''unpicked.''
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 397.}}}} '''3.''' Not picked or opened with an instrument, as a lock.

'''unpierceable''' (un-pēr′sa-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being pierced. ''Bp. Hall'', Saul in David’s Care.

'''unpierced''' (un-pērst′), ''a.'' Not pierced; not penetrated. ''Byron'', Mazeppa.

'''unpillared''' (un-pil′ärd), ''a.'' Deprived of pillars; not having or supported by pillars. ''Pope'', Dunciad, iii. 107.

'''unpilled†''' (un-pild′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pilled'', pp. of ''pill''<sup>1</sup>.] Unpillaged. ''Dr. Dee'', Petty Navy Royal (1576). (''Davies.'')

'''unpillowed''' (un-pil′ōd), ''a.'' Having no pillow; having the head not supported. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 353.

'''unpiloted''' (un-pī′lot-ed), ''a.'' Unguided through dangers or difficulties. ''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xxxv.

'''unpin''' (un-pin′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unpinned'', ppr. ''unpinning''. [< ME. ''unpynnen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''pin''<sup>1</sup>.] To remove the pin or pins that fasten. {{smaller|(''a'') To unbolt.}}
{{smaller block|He . . . gan the stewe dore al soft ''unpynne.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 698.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To unfasten or unloose by taking out the pins: as, to ''unpin'' a ribbon or a gown; hence, to loosen the garments of; undress.}}

{{smaller block|''Emil.'' Shall I go fetch your night-gown?
''Des.'' No, ''unpin'' me here. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 3. 35.}}}}
{{smaller block|The peremptory Analysis that you will call it, I beleeve will be so hardy as once more to ''unpinne'' your spruce fastidious oratory, to rumple her laces, her frizzles, and her bobins though she wince, and fling never so Peevishly.
{{right|''Milton'', Animadversions.}}}}

'''unpinion''' (un-pin′yon), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''pinion''<sup>1</sup>.] To loose from pinions or manacles; free from restraint. ''Clarke.''

'''unpinked†''' (un-pingkt′), ''a.'' Not pinked; not pierced with eyelet-holes. ''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 1. 136.

'''unpiteous''' (un-pit′ẹ̄-us), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unpitous'', ''unpietous''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''piteous''.] '''1†.''' Impious; wicked.—'''2.''' Pitiless; cruel.
{{smaller block|Myn ''unpietous'' lyf draweth a long unagreable dwellynges in me. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. meter 1.}}}}

'''unpiteously''' (un-pit′ẹ̄-us-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unpitously''; < ''unpiteous'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1†.''' Impiously; wickedly. ''Wyclif'', Ecclus. xlvi. 23.—'''2.''' In an unpiteous manner; cruelly.
{{smaller block|Oxford, in her senility, has proved no Alma Mater in thus so ''unpiteously'' cramming her alumni with the shells alone. {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}

'''unpiteousness''' (un-pit′ẹ̄-us-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unpitousnesse''; < ''unpiteous'' + ''-ness''.] '''1†.''' Impiety; wickedness. ''Wyclif'', Lev. xix. 7.—'''2.''' The character or state of being unpiteous or cruel.

'''unpitied''' (un-pit′id), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not pitied; not compassionated; not regarded with sympathetic sorrow.
{{smaller block|<poem>Go, and weep as I did,
And be ''unpitied.''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, iv. 3.}}}}
<poem>Stumbling across the market to his death
''Unpitied.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}} You shall have your full time of imprisonment and your deliverance with an ''unpitied'' whipping.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 2. 13.}}}}

{{right|''Sir J. Davies'', Wit’s Pilgrimage.}}}}

{{smaller block|Beat him most ''unpitifully.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 2. 215.}}}}

'''unpitifulness''' (un-pit′i-fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unpitiful. ''Sir P. Sidney,'' Arcadia, iii.

'''unpitous†''', etc. See ''unpiteous'', etc.

'''unpity†''', ''n.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pity.''] Impiety. ''Wyclif'', Rom. i. 18.

'''unpitying''' (un-pit′i-ing), ''a.'' Having no pity; showing no compassion.

'''unpityingly''' (un-pit′i-ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unpitying manner; without compassion.

'''unplace''' (un-plās′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''place.''] To displace.
{{smaller block|The papists do place in pre-eminence over the whole church the pope, thereby ''unplacing'' Christ, which is the Head of the church.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 142.}}}}

'''unplaced''' (un-plāst′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not arranged or distributed in proper places; undetermined in regard to place; confused; jumbled. {{smaller block|It is a thousand times more credible that four mutable elements and one immutable fifth essence, duly and eternally placed, need no God, than that an army of infinite small portions, or seeds ''unplaced'', should have produced this order and beauty without a divine marshal.
{{right|''Bacon'', Atheism (ed. 1887).}}}}
'''2.''' Having no place, office, or employment under government.
{{smaller block|''Unplaced'', unpension’d. ''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, ii. 1.}}

'''unplagued''' (un-plāgd′), ''a.'' Not plagued; not harassed; not tormented; not afflicted. ''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 5. 19.

'''unplain†''' (un-plān′), ''a.'' [ME. ''unplain''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''plain''<sup>1</sup>.] Not plain; not simple; not open; insincere. ''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i.

'''unplained†''' (un-plānd′), ''a.'' Not deplored; not bewailed or lamented.
{{smaller block|To die alone, unpitied, ''unplained''.
{{right|''Spenser'', Daphnaïda.}}}}

'''unplait''' (un-plāt′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unpleiten''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''plait''. Cf. ''unplight''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1†.''' To unfold; explain.
{{smaller block|Unnete may I ''unpleyten'' my sentence with wordes.

'''2.''' To undo the plaits of; unbraid: as, to ''unplait'' hair.
{{smaller block|One day she even went the length of ''unplaiting'' with swift warm fingers all the wavy coils of that rippling hair.

'''unplant''' (un-plant′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''plant''<sup>1</sup>.] To remove, as that which is planted; uproot; deprive of plants; hence, to depopulate.
{{smaller block|Being inioyned by our Commission not to ''vnplant'' nor wrong the Saluages, because the channell was so neere the shore where now is Iames Towne, then a thicke groue {{smaller block|of trees, wee cut them downe.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', True Travels, II. 99.}}}}

'''unplanted''' (un-plan′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not planted; of spontaneous growth. ''Waller'', Battle of the Islands, i.—'''2.''' Not cultivated; unimproved.
{{smaller block|Ireland is a country wholly ''unplanted.'' The farms have neither dwelling-houses nor good offices, nor are the lands anywhere provided with fences and communications.
{{right|''Burke'', On Popery Laws, iv.}}}}

'''unplastic''' (un-plas′tik), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not plastic; not readily molded. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XIX. 637.—'''2.''' Not suitable for plastic representation; unsculptural.
{{smaller block|Thoroughly ''unplastic'' in action and conception.
{{right|''C. C. Perkins'', Italian Sculpture, p. 244.}}}}

'''unplausible''' (un-plâ′zi-bl), ''a.'' Not plausible; not having a fair or specious appearance.
{{smaller block|Such ''unplausible'' propositions.
{{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, III. xlv.}}}}

'''unplausibly''' (un-plâ′zi-bli), ''adv.'' In an unplausible manner; not plausibly.
{{smaller block|Public suspicions which unjustly (but not altogether ''unplausibly'') taxed them with Popish leanings.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Secret Societies, I.}}}}

'''unplausive†''' (un-plâ′siv), ''a.'' Not approving; not applauding; displeased; disapproving.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis like he’ll question me
Why such ''unplausive'' eyes are bent on him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 3. 43.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
